title: Robert Molesworth, denouncer of Danish tyranny
gist: Felice Basbøll profiles Robert Molesworth, the Irish-born Whig envoy whose 1694 'Account of Denmark' cast Denmark's post-1660 absolutism as a cautionary tale for England: tyranny grows from a doctrine of blind obedience, arbitrary taxes for a standing army, and clerical control of education, not just 'popery'. His 'Principles of a Real Whig' (government of laws, not persons) shaped transatlantic Whig thought, and the author suggests he offers a lesson for liberals today.

insights.claim: Molesworth argued Denmark's post-1660 absolutism let the king consolidate power and levy arbitrary taxes to maintain a great standing army, while the people grew accustomed to their lack of liberty.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Concentrated executive power tends to bring arbitrary fiscal extraction, a long-run risk to property and capital.
insights.quote: the little Finger of an Absolute Prince can be heavier than the Loins of many Nobles

insights.claim: Molesworth held that the enemy of liberty is not a particular religion but the doctrine of blind obedience in whatever form it appears.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Institutional erosion can come from any ideology demanding unconditional deference, not only from familiar enemies.
insights.quote: but the doctrine of blind Obedience in what Religion soever it be found
insights.locator: Still, he sought to define tyranny

insights.claim: Molesworth blamed Danish absolutism partly on clerical control of education, arguing that entrusting youth to philosophers rather than priests might have helped resist tyranny.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Control over education shapes long-run political culture and institutional resilience.
insights.locator: Much of the Account is spent

insights.claim: Denmark's acquiescence followed general displeasure with the nobles after the war with Sweden, which led to popular support for the king's 1660 coup, after which nobles lost influence.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Populist backlash against elites can be the entry point for executive power grabs.

insights.claim: Molesworth thought that once a people accept absolutism they may change their masters but never their condition.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Institutional decline can be path-dependent and hard to reverse.
insights.quote: the People may with great difficulty change their Masters, but never their Condition

themes.theme: Principles of a 'real Whig' and liberal identity

insights.claim: Molesworth's 'Principles of a Real Whig' set out a constitution of laws not persons, frequent parliaments, religious toleration, and opposition to standing armies except when necessary to defend liberty.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Core rule-of-law tenets remain the benchmark for assessing institutional quality.
insights.quote: our Constitution is a Government of Laws, not of Persons
insights.locator: This preface, as Molesworth saw it

insights.claim: Molesworth warned that nominal Whigs without commitment to core principles were 'worse than any Sort of Men', and the author suggests his insistence on the label offers a lesson for liberals today.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Signals an intellectual push for liberals to reclaim clear principles amid shifting political labels.

insights.claim: Post-1688 political faultlines were reshaped by growing interest in foreign affairs, the founding of the Bank of England and the rise of the 'monied interest', which did not map onto old coalitions.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Financial innovation historically reconfigures political coalitions, a pattern relevant to today's realignments.

insights.claim: Molesworth's Account initially proved more popular than John Locke's Two Treatises on Government, and Denmark commissioned rebuttals that failed to dent its influence on European perceptions of Danes.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Shows the enduring reputational power of a well-told national narrative.
insights.locator: The bold and undeniably entertaining Account

insights.claim: After losing much of his money in the South Sea Bubble, Molesworth fronted the campaign to hold the company's directors to account.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Financial bubbles generate political backlash and accountability campaigns against corporate insiders.
